concept.name: Delta hedge
concept.definition: An options-hedging technique that offsets a position's delta - the theoretical sensitivity of the option's premium to a $1 move in the underlying - by taking an opposing position in the underlying, so the total position is approximately insensitive to small price moves.
concept.intuition: If your option gains $0.50 when the stock rises $1, shorting half a share per option makes the combined position roughly flat for small moves.
concept.mechanics: Delta is the first derivative of option value with respect to the underlying price (0 to 1 for long calls, 0 to -1 for long puts). A delta hedge sets total position delta to zero, e.g., shorting delta*N*100 shares against N long calls. Because delta changes as the underlying moves (gamma), the hedge must be rebalanced dynamically; Greeks are theoretical guideposts from a pricing model, not guarantees.
concept.formula: Position delta = sum over positions of (quantity * contract multiplier * delta_i); hedge shares = -position delta (per share delta of 1).
concept.failure_modes: Delta hedging is exact only locally and continuously: discrete rebalancing, gaps, and transaction costs leave residual P&L, and a delta-neutral book remains exposed to gamma (large moves), vega (volatility changes), and theta (time decay).
concept.misconceptions: Delta-neutral does not mean risk-neutral: it neutralizes only the first-order price exposure at one point in time, and delta is also not literally the probability of finishing in the money, despite the common trader shorthand.
concept.example: An investor long 10 calls with delta 0.50 shorts 500 shares (10 * 100 * 0.50); a $1 stock rise adds about $500 to the calls and loses about $500 on the shares, keeping the position near flat until delta changes.

citations.source: The Options Industry Council (OIC), Options Education: Delta
